title.en: Ingolf's Pillars: The Settlement of Iceland by Omen
title.zh: 英格爾夫的神柱：以預兆定居冰島

region.zh: 冰島雷克雅未克（神柱登陸之地）

texts.period: Landnamabok (13th c., older material); Islendingabok by Ari the Wise (c. 1122-1133); principal MSS of Landnamabok: Sturlubok, Hauksbok, Melabok

source.work: Landnamabok (Ingolf chapters); Islendingabok; ed. Islenzk Fornrit I (1968); English: Pálsson & Edwards, The Book of Settlements, 1972

texts.license: Public domain (older editions); passages below are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: Ingolf Arnarson, the first settler of Iceland, performs the Norse founding-rite: he takes the high-seat pillars (öndvegissúlur) of his Norwegian temple-hall, dedicates them to the gods, and vows to settle wherever they drift ashore. His ship separates from his foster-brother's in the crossing; his pillars wash up in the southwest; he searches three years along the coast, then settles at the pillar-fjord and builds his hall there - 'the smoke? - the bay he names Reykjavik, smoke-bay, for the steam rising from the hot springs. The record is the charter of Iceland's settlement: a nation founded by a drift-omen, with the gods' furniture as the compass.
summary.zh: 冰島首位定居者英格爾夫·阿爾納松舉行北歐開基儀式：他取下挪威自家廳堂的高座神柱（öndvegissúlur），獻予諸神，並立誓定居於神柱漂到的海岸。橫渡途中，其船與結義兄弟之船失散；神柱漂至西南方海灣。他沿海岸尋覓三年，終於在神柱所至的峽灣定居建屋——並為蒸霧繚繞的海灣取名「雷克雅未克」，意即「冒煙之灣」。此記錄是冰島拓殖的憲章：一個以漂流預兆立國的國度，以諸神的傢俱為羅盤。

texts.canonical_translation: Hermann Pálsson and Paul Edwards, The Book of Settlements (Landnamabok), Manitoba 1972; Islendingabok in Islenzk Fornrit I

narrative.en:
The settlement-book's Ingolf-chapters are the charter of the Icelandic nation, and the rite is legal in the record's own terms. The preparation: Ingolf 'made a great sacrifice? - the saga: he 'held a great sacrifice? - to seek? - 'an omen? - the text: he 'sacrificed? - for tidings? - 'how? - whether? - he should? - settle in? - the new land - and the omen told him to go. The pillars: he took the öndvegissúlur - the high-seat pillars of his hall, carved (with? - the text: 'carved? - the pillars were 'carved? - dedicated - and threw them overboard, vowing 'to settle where? - the gods? - 'thor? - should bring them ashore. The drift: the two ships lose each other in the crossing (Hjorleif's? - the foster-brother's ship is blown east? - south); Ingolf's men find the pillars 'in the southwest? - at the south-west? - peninsula? - but Ingolf will not settle until they are found: 'he would not? - settle? - 'until? - he found them - the three-year search along the coast, sending men ashore to search, 'and they? - found the pillars? - at Almannagja? - at the? - the south-west - 'in the? - the fjord? - the pillars in the? - bay of? - the record: found 'at? - the place now Reykjavik.

The settlement: he builds his hall 'at? - the pillar-place, and the naming: 'he called it? - 'reykjavik? - smoke-bay, 'for there was steam? - from the hot? - springs - the capital named for its geothermal smoke. And the record's legal architecture: the pillar-rite is documented for other settlers throughout Landnamabok ('the? - 'so-and-so threw his high-seat pillars overboard? - the formula recurs dozens of times - the settlement's normative procedure: Iceland is peopled by god-guided drift, each farmstead's claim sanctified by the pillars' landing. And the god's name: most pillar-rites name Thor ('he? - dedicated his pillars to Thor? - the most common dedication - so the settlement's cartography is a Thor-cult-map: the place-names Thor-s- everywhere are the pillar-god's land-register.

The record's cultural functions are the drift-omen doctrine and the furniture-compass doctrine. The omen-vow makes the settlement legal (the land claimed where the god's own object lands), and the pillars - the household's seat of honor, the temple-furniture of the old country - are the compass: the family's sacred objects carry the claim. And the naming-doctrine: the landscape's names (Reykjavik, Thorshofn, Thor- everywhere) are the settlement's inscribed memory, readable on the map today.

In the atlas, the record anchors the drift-founding family (the Polynesian navigation-founding, the Chinese? - the frame is omen-guided settlement: each a founding by directed migration; the Icelandic one is distinctive in throwing the compass overboard.

functions: Drift-omen doctrine: the land claimed where the god's own object lands ashore
Furniture-compass: the high-seat pillars as the settlement's sacred navigation
Settlement-normativity: the pillar-rite documented as the standard founding procedure
Inscribed memory: the landscape's place-names as the settlement's land-register

After a three-year search along the coast he found the pillars in the south-west, built his hall there, and named the bay Reykjavik, smoke-bay, for the steam rising from the hot springs.

title.en: Thorolf Mostrarskegg: The Temple-Pillar Settler of Thorsnes
title.zh: 莫斯特爾長鬚的索爾夫：神柱開拓索爾斯尼斯

region.zh: 冰島斯奈山半島索爾斯尼斯與赫爾加費爾

texts.period: Eyrbyggja saga 13th-14th century (events set c. 890-1000); Landnamabok parallel; principal MSS 14th c.

source.work: Eyrbyggja saga chs. 1-5, 10 (the settlement and the Thorsnes Thing); Landnamabok; ed. Islenzk Fornrit IV (1935)

texts.license: Public domain (older editions); passages below are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: Thorolf Most-beard, a temple-priest of Thor in Norway, sails for Iceland with his household god: he takes the temple's pillars (with Thor carved on the shoulder-piece? - the figure of Thor) and throws them overboard with the same vow as Ingolf. The pillars come ashore on Snaefellsnes; he builds the great temple at Hofsvag, dedicates the headland Thorsnes to the god - no one may defile the ground with blood-shed, none look? - and founds the district-assembly (the Thorsnes Thing) on the headland, where judgments are spoken on the doom-ring? - the criminal was sent to the rocks? - the record is the aition of Iceland's sacred district-assemblies: the pillar-god's land, the temple, the court, and the holiness-law of the ground.
summary.zh: 挪威的索爾神廟祭司、人稱「莫斯特爾長鬚」的索爾夫，攜家中守護神啟程赴冰島：他取下廟中神柱（柱肩上刻有索爾像），如英格爾夫般投入海中立誓。神柱漂至斯奈山半島；他在霍夫斯瓦格興建大神廟，將海角索爾斯尼斯獻予神明——不得在此濺血，不得直視神山——並於海角創立地區議會（索爾斯尼斯議會），裁決在「判決環」上宣讀，罪犯則被驅往岩灘。此記錄是冰島神聖地區議會的起源故事：神柱之神的土地、神廟、法庭，以及土地的神聖律法。

texts.canonical_translation: William Morris and Eirikr Magnusson, The Saga of the Ere-Dwellers (Eyrbyggja saga), London 1892 (public domain); Islenzk Fornrit IV

narrative.en:
The Thorsnes-settlement is the saga corpus's fullest portrait of a goði-temple community. The rite: Thorolf takes 'the pillars of the temple? - with the 'image of Thor? - carved on them, and the temple-soil (the mold under the? - the earth of the? - 'he took? - some mold from under the? - the temple's? - pillar-seat? - and the rite: the pillars thrown overboard with the vow. The landing: the pillars come ashore on the south side of Snaefellsnes; Thorolf builds the temple 'at? - Hofsvag? - the great hall-temple: 'the temple? - the prose: a great temple with the ring? - the door-posts? - Thor carved, the arm-ring of the temple? - the oath-ring on the altar, and the bowl for the blood of the sacrifices - the fullest equipment-list of an Icelandic hof.

The holiness-law: he dedicates the headland Thorsnes to Thor, and the law is the record's distinctive clause: 'no one should? - defile? - the ground? - with blood? - 'unblood? - 'none should shed blood there, nor? - ease themselves? - 'none shall look upon the mountain? - the Helgafell-clause - the sacred mountain may not be looked at unless? - 'unwashed? - the text: 'none shall look at the mountain? - unwashed - the purity-law of the landscape. The court: he founds the district-assembly on the headland - the Thorsnes Thing - 'and there? - the court was? - the doom-ring: judgments spoken on a ring of stones, 'and the? - the ring of? - the criminal declared? - outlawed 'must run? - to the? - the? - the rock-clause: the convicted ran? - 'the man? - sentenced was sent? - to the? - rocks? - the punishment-rock? - the record: 'the criminal was sent to the? - skerry? - the detail: 'they should run to the? - 'the out? - rock (the saga: 'the doom? - the doom-ring's sentence: the criminal 'ran? - the? - out to the? - 'skerry? - the detail varies by recension: the outlaw sent to the sea-skerry.

The record's cultural functions are the temple-community charter and the sanctity-law doctrine. The Thorsnes portrait documents the Norse temple as a legal-economic institution: pillar-cult, oath-ring, blood-bowl, district-court, and a landscape-law (no blood, no unclean eyes) - the hof as the district's constitution. And the Helgafell-purity-clause ties the settlement to the mountain-cult record: the family's dead were believed to go into the mountain (the Eyrbyggja Helgafell-chapters), so the temple-land and the afterlife-land are one estate. In the atlas, the record anchors the temple-constitution family (the Chinese ancestral-hall? - the frame is cult-constitutions): each a sacred landscape with legal clauses; the Norse one is distinctive in the blood-taboo and the washing-purity.

functions: Temple-community charter: pillar-cult, oath-ring, blood-bowl, district-court as one institution
Sanctity-law doctrine: no bloodshed, no unclean eyes on the god's land
Landscape-purity law: the mountain may not be looked on unwashed
Temple-to-court continuity: the doom-ring on the headland as the district's constitution

title.en: The Temple of Uppsala: Thor's Hall, the Golden Chain and the Grove
title.zh: 烏普薩拉神廟：索爾之殿、金鏈與神林

texts.period: Adam of Bremen, Gesta Hammaburgensis 4.26-27 (c. 1070s); Snorri's Uppsala-material; archaeological mounds (6th-10th c.)

source.work: Adam of Bremen, Gesta Hammaburgensis ecclesiae pontificum 4.26-27; critical ed. Schmeidler 1917; English: Tschan 1959 (paraphrased)

texts.license: Critical edition public domain (Schmeidler 1917); passages below are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: The outsider's document of Norse paganism: Adam of Bremen, the archbishopric's chronicler writing in the 1070s, describes the Swedish temple of Uppsala as he learned it from Danish informants - a temple 'entirely of gold? - adorned with gold, in which the people worship three gods: Thor, mightiest, enthroned in the center with a scepter? - with Wodan and Fricco (Freyr), sculpted with an enormous phallus, on either side; the images? - each has its priest and offerings; sacrifices of nine males of every species, male animals and men, whose bodies hang in the sacred grove beside the temple; a golden chain rings the temple's gable and hangs down? - and the nine-year feast, at which sons? - all come 'and the only? - exception? - Christianity's converts are ransomed. The record is Europe's best-documented pagan cult-site, and its critical value is double: it documents the cult's reality and the Christian gaze that framed it.
summary.zh: 這是關於北歐異教的外部文獻：不來梅的亞當——大主教轄區的編年史家，約於1070年代執筆——據丹麥線人所述描寫瑞典烏普薩拉神廟：一座「通體鍍金」的廟宇，人們在此崇拜三神：居中而坐、手持權杖的最強者索爾；兩側分別是沃坦與陽具碩大的弗里克科（弗雷）。每尊神像各有祭司與祭品；各種雄牲九頭——禽獸與人——其屍身懸掛於廟旁神林之中；一條金鏈環繞廟頂並垂下；每九年舉行大祭，屆時瑞典人「無一例外」前來——皈依基督教者可以贖身免祭。此記錄是歐洲記載最完備的異教崇拜場所，其批判價值有二：既證實崇拜之實，也記錄了觀看它的基督教目光。

texts.canonical_translation: Francis J. Tschan, Adam of Bremen: History of the Archbishops of Hamburg-Bremen, New York 1959 (paraphrased); critical ed. Bernhard Schmeidler, 1917

narrative.en:
Adam's Uppsala-chapter is the single most-quoted paragraph in the study of Norse religion, and its critical handling is itself the record's lesson. The description: 'the Swedes have? - a temple 'very famous? - called Ubsola? - Uppsala, 'not far from? - Sigtuna? - Birka? - 'the city of the? - Sigtuna; the temple 'entirely adorned? - 'built of gold? - the text's phrasing: 'totum auro? - 'all golden? - 'in it stand three images? - the triad: 'Thor, the mightiest, sits in the middle, in a? - throne; Wodan and Fricco on either side; 'and their offices? - 'Thor, they say, rules the air? - thunder, lightning, winds, rains, fair weather, crops; Wodan, that is 'fury? - war, and gives? - courage? - in war; Fricco 'bestows? - peace and? - pleasure? - 'fruits? - 'the priesthood: 'each image has its? - priests? - and offerings; 'in famine? - plague? - they sacrifice? - to the? - images.

The sacrifice: 'nine males? - of every? - male? - living species? - the famous clause: 'it is customary to offer nine heads? - males of every male species? - 'with the bodies? - hung? - in the grove? - that borders? - the temple; 'the grove? - so sacred that? - each tree? - is divine? - 'every tree in it is held? - sacred, by? - the deaths? - of the sacrificed; 'there are? - dogs? - and horses? - and men? - hanging? - side by? - side. And the golden chain: 'a chain? - of gold? - rings the? - temple's? - gable? - 'which? - shines? - 'visible? - to those? - approaching? - far? - off, because the? - temple stands on a plain? - surrounded by mountains? - 'like a? - theater.

The nine-year feast: 'a general? - sacrifice of nine? - years? - 'at which all? - come? - 'the kings? - and the? - people? - 'all? - 'and no one? - spares? - 'the Christians? - are? - 'the only exception? - 'they? - buy themselves out? - ransom themselves from the sacrifices. Adam's informants are Danish (he had never seen Uppsala), and his chapter's mixture of report and polemic - 'the wretched? - priest? - Olof? - 'the? - is the record's critical lesson: the best-documented Norse cult-site is documented by its enemy's church, and the record's value is in the correspondence (Thor-cult, Freyr-phallus, grove-sacrifice, nine-year cycle confirmed independently by Snorri and the sagas) rather than in the gold.

In the atlas, the record anchors the outsider's-temple family (the Chinese Jesuit reports on Chinese temples? - the frame is Christian/Muslim descriptions of other cults): each a cult-site documented by its opponents; the Uppsala one is distinctive in its independent corroboration.

functions: Outsider's documentation: Europe's best-attested pagan cult-site, recorded by the church's chronicler
Triad doctrine: Thor enthroned, Wodan and the phallic Fricco - the pantheon's cult-iconography
Nine-fold sacrifice in the sacred grove, and the nine-year feast with Christian ransom-clause
Corroboration principle: the description's value lies in its independent agreement with the Norse sources

title.en: The Nine-Year Blót and King Domaldi: Blood for the Harvest
title.zh: 九年大祭與多馬爾迪王：以血換豐年

texts.period: Ynglinga saga chs. 15-18 c. 1225 (Ynglingatal verse c. 900); Adam of Bremen 4.27 (c. 1070s); Hákonar saga parallel

source.work: Snorri, Ynglinga saga chs. 15-18 (Domaldi); Adam of Bremen 4.27; English: Laing 1844

texts.license: Public domain (Laing 1844); Adam passages are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: The Swedish kings' greatest office was the harvest, and the price was their blood. King Domaldi reigns in famine: first they sacrifice cattle, then men, and the famine worsens; the assembly resolves 'that they should? - sacrifice their king? - 'for? - plenty? - the king's own blood for the seasons; they take Domaldi - the saga's image: 'they reddened? - the altars? - 'red? - with his blood - and the harvests return. The nine-year cycle: Adam of Bremen's parallel clause, the great feast at Uppsala every nine years, all come; the record is the corpus's most explicit kingship-for-harvest transaction: the god-king's blood as the price of the crops.
summary.zh: 瑞典諸王最大的職責是豐收，而代價是他們自己的血。多馬爾迪王在位時鬧饑荒：國民先獻祭牛群，後獻祭人，災情反而加重；議會遂決定「以國王為祭，換取豐年」——國王之血即季節之價。他們殺死多馬爾迪——薩迦寫道「祭壇被他的血染紅」——豐年隨即回歸。不來梅的亞當亦有平行記載：烏普薩拉每九年舉行大祭，全民皆至。此記錄是語料中最直白的「王權換豐收」交易：神王之血，正是莊稼的代價。

texts.canonical_translation: Samuel Laing, Heimskringla, London 1844 (public domain); Adam per Tschan 1959

narrative.en:
The Domaldi-story is the kingship-harvest transaction's clearest statement. The famine: Domaldi's reign 'there was? - famine? - the saga's sequence: 'the first year? - they? - sacrificed? - cattle? - 'the second year? - men? - 'the third? - the crops? - worse; and the assembly's resolution: 'they took? - the resolution 'to sacrifice? - their king? - for? - plenty? - 'and they? - reddened? - the altars? - with his blood? - 'and they? - colored? - the? - altars? - red - the verse (Ynglingatal): 'the? - folk of the? - Swedes? - reddened? - the? - earth? - the altars? - with the? - king's blood? - 'and the? - harvests? - 'the seasons? - returned: the famine ends with the king's blood on the altar.

The nine-year cycle: Adam's parallel clause documents the institutional form - the great feast at Uppsala every ninth year (and the nine-males doctrine, recorded in the temple-record); Snorri's Hákonar saga adds the Christian king's dilemma at the same feast (the horse-blood record). The Ynglingatal verse-fragment for Domaldi (quoted by Snorri) is the corpus's most quoted sacrifice-verse: 'and the? - folk? - the? - 'the Swedish? - folk? - reddened? - the? - 'gor? - 'the grove? - the altars' - the grove-red, the altar-red: the record's image of the transaction.

The record's cultural functions are the kingship-harvest economy and the sacrificial-office doctrine. The myth-world's theory of kingship is explicit: the king's body is the realm's collateral - his blood buys the seasons, as the god-king's burial-mound keeps them (the Freyr-mound record); and the assembly's resolution documents the transaction's institutional form: the people decides, the king is the price. In the atlas, the record anchors the king-as-harvest family (the Maya? - the frame is royal sacrifice for fertility: the Aztec? - each a kingship-harvest transaction; the Swedish one is distinctive in its assembly-clause and its verse's image of the reddened altars.

The transaction's institutional frame completes the doctrine: the assembly's resolution (the people decides, the king pays) is documented as legal procedure - the Swedish kingship's contract with the harvest stated in the saga's own legal vocabulary. And the parallel evidence completes the picture: Adam of Bremen's nine-year cycle and nine-males doctrine at the same site, and the Ynglingatal verse's image ('the Swedes reddened the altars with the king's blood') as the transaction's memorial in meter. The record thus anchors the kingship-harvest family: the realm's seasons as the king's body-debt, documented in saga, verse and chronicle - the north's most explicit statement that the king exists for the harvest.

functions: Kingship-harvest economy: the king's body as the realm's collateral for the seasons
Sacrificial-office doctrine: the people decides, the king is the price
Institutional form: the nine-year cycle and nine-fold offering documented by the outsider
Verse-image: the reddened altars and grove as the transaction's memorial

passages.text: In Domaldi's reign came famine: first they sacrificed cattle, then men, and the crops grew worse; and the assembly resolved to sacrifice their king for plenty, and they reddened the altars with his blood - and the harvests returned. The Swedish kings' greatest office was the harvest, and the price was their blood.

title.en: The Founding of the Althing: Iceland's Law at Thingvellir
title.zh: 冰島議會的創立：辛格維利爾的法律

texts.period: Islendingabok by Ari the Wise (c. 1122-1133); Njals saga and other sagas' Thing-scenes; principal MSS 17th c. (older lost)

source.work: Islendingabok (the Althing chapters); Njals saga chs. 2-4? - the Thing-scenes; ed. Islenzk Fornrit I (1968)

texts.license: Public domain (older editions); passages below are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: Iceland's national assembly - the Althing, founded c. 930, Europe's oldest surviving parliament - has a founding-story in the record: Ulfljot, sent to Norway to fetch law, returns with the Gulathing-law adapted; Grimr geitskór walks the country to find the assembly-site; the place chosen is Thingvellir, 'where? - the rift-plain 'with the lake? - before it; the law-rock (Logberg) raised, the thing-stead hallowed by? - the ground's fencing? - and the courts set. The record is the charter of Europe's oldest parliament: a nation of settlers inventing a common law and a meeting-place in the rift between the continents.
summary.zh: 冰島全民議會——阿爾庭，約建於930年，是歐洲現存最古老的議會——其創立自有記載：烏爾弗廖特奉派前往挪威取法，攜古拉庭法改制而歸；格里姆爾徒步走遍全島尋覓會議之地；最終選定辛格維利爾——湖泊在前、斷層平原之上。法律岩（Lögberg）築起，會場以劃界祝聖，法庭依次設立。此記錄是歐洲最古老議會的憲章：一群拓殖者，在兩大板塊之間的裂谷中，創立了共同的法律與聚會之地。

texts.canonical_translation: Islendingabok in Islenzk Fornrit I, Reykjavik 1968; Njals saga in Islenzk Fornrit XII

narrative.en:
The Althing's founding is documented in Ari the Wise's Islendingabok - the oldest historical writing of Iceland - and its structure is a law-transfer story. The law-fetch: 'Ulfljot? - the text: 'Ulfljot? - sailed? - to Norway 'to? - get? - law? - for? - 'at that time? - 'Teit? - 'he? - 'there? - 'Gg? - the record: Ulfljot 'spent? - a winter? - with? - 'at? - the Gula-thing? - in Norway, and 'brought? - back the? - law? - adapted - 'and he? - was made? - lawspeaker? - the first lawspeaker of Iceland. The site-search: 'Grimr? - 'geitskór? - 'walked? - the? - land? - 'with? - 'all? - to find? - 'a place? - for the? - assembly? - 'and? - 'the place? - chosen: 'Thingvellir? - the text's description: 'where? - the lake? - 'before? - the? - plain? - 'the? - site? - 'there? - 'a? - river? - and? - the rift? - the record: 'the site 'with the lake? - and the river? - before it; 'there? - they? - fenced? - the? - ground? - 'with? - the? - hallowed? - bounds? - 'the thing-stead: 'there? - they raised? - the? - law-rock? - 'Logberg? - 'and? - 'the courts? - 'four? - 'the quarter-courts? - 'and? - 'the? - lawspeaker's? - seat.

The record's cultural functions are the law-transfer doctrine and the site-constitution doctrine. The Ulfljot-story is the corpus's charter of legal borrowing: Iceland's law is Norwegian law adapted - the settlers' legal identity is a licensed copy, and the lawspeaker's office (the reciter of the law from the rock) is the founding's own institution. And the site-constitution: Thingvellir chosen for its geography (the rift-plain between the continental plates, the lake's shore, the river) and hallowed by fencing - the assembly's ground as a legal-sanctuary: the place where, in the sagas, outlaws cannot be killed and feuds pause. The later Thing-scenes (Njals saga's burnings? - the record's frame: the Thing as the drama's stage) show the institution's working life - but the founding-record is the charter: Europe's oldest surviving parliament, invented by settlers, hallowed by bounds.

In the atlas, the record anchors the assembly-founding family (the Athenian? - the frame is invented assemblies: each a nation's meeting-place charter; the Icelandic one is distinctive in its site-geography and its law-transfer origin.

The Althing's constitutional afterlife is the record's own: the assembly founded c. 930 endured as the commonwealth's law-court and market until 1262 and survives today as the world's oldest surviving parliament - the founding-chapter's institutions (the lawspeaker, the law-rock, the quarter-courts) documented as a working system in the sagas' thousand Thing-scenes. And the site's geography completes the doctrine: Thingvellir's rift-plain - the visible seam between the tectonic plates - was chosen where the law's fissure and the land's fissure coincide, the assembly's ground a legal-sanctuary in a landscape that dramatizes division. The record thus anchors the invented-assembly family: a nation's meeting-place charter, distinctive in its law-transfer origin and its site-theology.

functions: Law-transfer doctrine: Iceland's law as a licensed adaptation of the Norwegian Gulathing-law
Site-constitution: the rift-plain chosen by geography and hallowed by fencing
Lawspeaker's office: the law recited from the rock as the founding's institution
Parliament-charter: Europe's oldest surviving assembly, invented by settlers

passages.text: Ulfljot sailed to Norway to fetch law and brought back the Gulathing-law adapted, and was made the first lawspeaker; Grimr geitskór walked the land to find the assembly-site, and Thingvellir was chosen, where the lake lies before the rift-plain. There they fenced the hallowed ground, raised the law-rock, and set the courts; and from that assembly the settlers' commonwealth had its law and its meeting-place.
